lesson.title: Counting What Matters: The Sample Proportion
lesson.summary: The sample proportion is the fraction of individuals in a sample that fall into a category of interest, and it is the standard statistic used to estimate an unknown population proportion.
lesson.body:
Many questions in statistics are about categorical variables rather than numeric ones: does a voter support a proposition or not, does a manufactured part pass inspection or not, does a patient respond to a treatment or not. Each individual falls into one of two categories, success or failure, and we usually care about what fraction of the whole population would be a success. That population fraction is a parameter, denoted p, and because we can almost never survey an entire population, we estimate it using a sample.

The sample proportion, written p-hat, is calculated by taking a sample of size n, counting the number of successes in that sample, and dividing by n. If X is the count of successes, then p-hat equals X divided by n. Because p-hat is computed entirely from the data in hand, it is a statistic, just like the sample mean or sample standard deviation, and like any statistic it will vary from sample to sample even when the underlying population does not change.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a school wants to know what fraction of its 3000 students bike to school, and a researcher samples 200 students at random. Of those 200, 74 report biking to school. The sample proportion is p-hat = 74 / 200 = 0.37, or 37 percent. That number, 0.37, is a statistic: it describes this particular sample, and it is the researcher's best single estimate of the true population proportion p, which remains unknown unless every one of the 3000 students is surveyed.

It is worth being precise about what varies and what does not. The population proportion p is a fixed, if unknown, number: it does not change depending on who happens to get sampled. The sample proportion p-hat, on the other hand, depends entirely on which 200 students were selected. A different random sample of 200 students would very likely produce a different count of bikers, and therefore a different p-hat, perhaps 0.34 or 0.41 instead of 0.37. That sample-to-sample variability is exactly what the next chapter formalizes.
